summary:
Meta Department, a southern Colombian department in which an armed-conflict displacement dynamic persists, stands under Colombia's national framework. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. A national LGBTI policy addresses rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and states that national entities may not refuse to recognise them.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 1993 on the basis of self-recognition and without psychiatric or physical evaluations. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The formal framework meets a rising national pattern of violence. On 6 August 2025 an international broadcaster reported a wave of anti-LGBTQ attacks across Colombia, covered through the case of Sara Millerey, 32, who on 5 April 2025 was filmed flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups. An international investigation published on 30 July 2024 documents groups in Caquetá giving trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; she was forced to move twice. The same investigation quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and records these killings as ordinary cases, and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

No source in the inventory supplies a department-level record for Meta Department. Its entry rests on the national armed-group violence and displacement baseline and on the national legal provisions above, which is the layer a visitor there is governed by.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia was the fourth Latin American country to legalise same-sex marriage, in April 2016, and its formal position sits at the front of the region. The gap between that standing and enforcement is the finding of the May 2025 UN Independent Expert mission, which recorded institutional progress alongside widespread discrimination and violence as killings rise.

The violence documented in Caquetá is conflict-derived rather than ordinary crime: armed groups announce "social cleansing" campaigns against named trans women, and in Guajira they publish kill lists describing the listed people as military targets. Reporting on the Millerey case describes calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, and killings of queer Colombians continued after it.

Impediments to accountability are procedural as much as violent. An activist quoted in the 30 July 2024 investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording those killings as ordinary cases; the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment of 15 former rebels in July 2023 shows that the same conduct is charged as gender persecution and a crime against humanity when it reaches the transitional-justice track.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory supplies department-level detail for Meta Department. Its record here rests on the national legal baseline and on national armed-group violence and displacement patterns, with Caquetá and Guajira cited as documented examples of that pattern rather than as evidence about Meta itself.

The count of 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 comes from one investigation published on 30 July 2024; other sources describe the same year as more than 40. Both figures are retained as sourced rather than reconciled.

Claims that a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, and that a Colombian court issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees after 2011, appear in the record's continuity text without a date, court or citation in the current source inventory. They are stated as unresolved and not independently verifiable here.

Whether Meta Department's own police, prosecutors or detaining facilities apply the national rulings above is not sourced. Verification would require department-level reporting from Villavicencio or Meta's municipal authorities.
